title: Storage Redundancy Models
summary: Where Azure Storage keeps its copies for LRS, ZRS, GRS and GZRS — and what each survives.

nodes.label: LRS
nodes.detail: Locally redundant: 3 synchronous copies in one datacenter. Survives disk/rack failures, not a datacenter or zone outage.

nodes.label: Datacenter
nodes.detail: All three copies live in a single datacenter in the primary region.

nodes.label: ZRS
nodes.detail: Zone-redundant: 3 synchronous copies across three availability zones. Survives a zone outage.

nodes.label: Zone 1
nodes.detail: Each zone is a separate datacenter with independent power, cooling and networking.

nodes.label: Zone 2
nodes.detail: Writes succeed only after all three zones have the data (synchronous).

nodes.label: Zone 3
nodes.detail: If one zone fails, reads and writes continue from the other zones.

nodes.label: GRS
nodes.detail: Geo-redundant: LRS in the primary region plus asynchronous replication to the paired region. RA-GRS adds read access to the secondary.

nodes.label: Datacenter
nodes.detail: Primary copies are LRS — a single datacenter.

nodes.label: Datacenter
nodes.detail: The secondary region always stores data with LRS. Not readable unless you use RA-GRS or fail over.

nodes.label: GZRS
nodes.detail: Geo-zone-redundant: ZRS in the primary region plus asynchronous replication to the paired region. RA-GZRS adds read access.

nodes.label: Zone 1
nodes.detail: Zone-redundant primary copies, as with ZRS.

nodes.label: Zone 2
nodes.detail: Zone-redundant primary copies, as with ZRS.

nodes.label: Zone 3
nodes.detail: Zone-redundant primary copies, as with ZRS.

nodes.label: Datacenter
nodes.detail: Again LRS in the secondary region.

steps.title: LRS
steps.text: Three copies in one datacenter. Cheapest; doesn't survive a datacenter failure.

steps.title: ZRS
steps.text: One copy in each of three zones. Data stays available if a zone fails.

steps.title: GRS
steps.text: LRS in the primary plus an asynchronous copy (LRS) in the paired region. Survives a regional disaster after failover.

steps.title: GZRS
steps.text: Zone resilience in the primary region plus a geo copy — the most durable option.

examExpects: Match the failure to survive with the option: datacenter/zone → ZRS; region → GRS/GZRS; read during regional outage → RA-GRS/RA-GZRS.
Geo-replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose recent writes.
The secondary region always uses LRS.
Premium accounts support only LRS and ZRS.

title: Availability Sets vs Availability Zones
summary: Fault and update domains inside one datacenter versus VMs spread across physically separate zones.

nodes.label: VM1
nodes.detail: Fault domains are racks with separate power and network. If rack FD0 fails, only VMs in FD0 go down.

nodes.label: VM4
nodes.detail: VMs are distributed round-robin across fault and update domains as they're created.

nodes.label: VM2
nodes.detail: Update domains are rebooted one at a time during planned maintenance.

nodes.label: VM5
nodes.detail: With 5 update domains (the default), the 6th VM would go back into UD0.

nodes.label: VM3
nodes.detail: Availability sets protect against rack failures and planned maintenance, but not against a whole datacenter outage.

nodes.label: VM-A
nodes.detail: Each zone is a separate datacenter. A zone outage takes down only VMs in that zone.

nodes.label: VM-B
nodes.detail: Deploy at least two VMs in different zones to qualify for the highest VM SLA.

nodes.label: VM-C
nodes.detail: Three zones give room for one zone to fail while two keep serving.

nodes.label: Standard LB
nodes.detail: A zone-redundant Standard Load Balancer and Standard public IP keep the frontend available if a zone fails.

steps.title: Fault domains
steps.text: An availability set spreads VMs across up to three fault domains (racks) so a hardware failure affects only some of them.

steps.title: Update domains
steps.text: Planned maintenance reboots one update domain at a time. VM1 (UD0) and VM2 (UD1) never reboot together.

steps.title: Availability zones
steps.text: Zones are separate datacenters. Spreading VMs across zones survives a full datacenter outage.

steps.title: Front it with a load balancer
steps.text: A zone-redundant Standard LB distributes traffic only to healthy VMs in surviving zones.

examExpects: Availability sets: fault domains (unplanned hardware failure) and update domains (planned maintenance) in one datacenter.
Availability zones: separate datacenters in a region; highest VM SLA with 2+ VMs across zones.
You choose the availability option at VM creation; you can't add an existing VM to a set.
Neither option protects against a regional outage — use Site Recovery or multi-region designs.

title: VM Scale Sets & Autoscale
summary: How metrics drive autoscale rules that add and remove load-balanced scale set instances.

nodes.label: Users
nodes.detail: Client requests arrive at the load balancer's frontend.

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.detail: The scale set registers instances in the backend pool; the probe ensures only healthy instances get traffic.

nodes.label: Instance 1
nodes.detail: Instances are created from the scale set model (image, size, extensions).

nodes.label: Instance 2
nodes.detail: Minimum instance count is always maintained.

nodes.label: Instance 3
nodes.detail: Added automatically when the scale-out rule fired. It will be removed when the scale-in rule fires (respecting the scale-in policy).

nodes.label: Azure Monitor
nodes.detail: Host metrics such as Percentage CPU are collected automatically; guest metrics need an agent.

nodes.label: Autoscale setting
nodes.detail: Profile with min/max/default, scale-out and scale-in rules, cooldown, and optional schedules.

steps.title: Traffic
steps.text: Users hit the load balancer, which spreads requests across healthy instances.

steps.title: Metrics
steps.text: Instances emit CPU metrics to Azure Monitor.

steps.title: Rule evaluation
steps.text: Autoscale evaluates rules: average CPU above 70% for 10 minutes triggers scale-out.

steps.title: Scale out
steps.text: A new instance is added (up to the maximum) and joins the backend pool automatically. A paired scale-in rule removes it when load drops.

examExpects: Autoscale needs both scale-out and scale-in rules, bounded by min and max counts.
Use schedule-based profiles for predictable load patterns.
Scale-in policy controls which instances are removed first.
Scale sets integrate with Load Balancer or Application Gateway backend pools automatically.
